title: Macrocytic Anemia: B12, Folate and Hydroxyurea
summary: Learn why vitamin B12 must be checked before folate is given for a megaloblastic anemia, how to read borderline B12 results with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, and how drugs such as hydroxyurea raise the MCV with normal vitamin levels.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 33 Hit 3 (B12 deficiency is neurologic; never folate alone; confirm borderline B12 with MMA/homocysteine), Hit 16 (hydroxyurea macrocytosis) and Exam Trap 3 (folate for a megaloblastic smear). Checked against Nagao 2017, Wolffenbuttel 2019, Hannibal 2016, Aslinia 2006 (read via a page-fetch tool), Green 2014 and Quinn 2025. Hit 3 is qualified (register flag rv-ch33-b12-borderline-range): the sources read put the borderline zone at 200–300 pg/mL (Nagao 2017) or 140–300 pmol/L (Wolffenbuttel 2019), not 100–200 ng/L, and below 200 pg/mL deficiency is already very likely. Hit 16 is qualified (register flag rv-ch33-hydroxyurea-not-reliably-nonmegaloblastic): hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and Nagao 2017 states megaloblastic smear features, including hypersegmented neutrophils, can also be seen in drug-induced disorders of DNA synthesis; Nagao 2017 starts the macrocytosis workup with B12, folate and the smear, and places hypothyroidism among the causes considered after vitamin deficiency is excluded (register flag rv-ch33-macrocytosis-first-tests). Trap 3’s “methionine/SAM pathway for myelin” mechanism is not taught: Wolffenbuttel 2019 states why some patients present with nerve damage and others with anemia remains unknown.

objectives: Explain why vitamin B12 deficiency, but not generally folate deficiency, causes neurologic damage, and why folate alone is hazardous in B12 deficiency.
Interpret serum B12 cutoffs and use methylmalonic acid and homocysteine to resolve borderline results, including their pitfalls.
Recognise hydroxyurea and other drugs as causes of macrocytosis and why the smear alone does not separate them from vitamin deficiency.

scenes.title: Three big red cells
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three adults with macrocytosis. (1) A 68-year-old woman, MCV 112 fL, numb feet and an unsteady gait, serum B12 240 pg/mL, already started on folic acid by another clinic. (2) A 59-year-old man on hydroxyurea for essential thrombocythemia, MCV 118 fL, serum B12 and folate normal. (3) A 47-year-old with tingling hands, normal hemoglobin and MCV, low serum B12. Question token: “Who must not get folate alone?”

cues.text: Three adults with big red cells, or nerve symptoms. The first is sixty-eight, with numb feet, an unsteady gait, a borderline B12, and she has already been started on folic acid.
The second takes hydroxyurea and has a very high MCV with normal B12 and folate. The third has tingling hands, a normal blood count, and a low B12.
Who must not get folate alone, and whose big cells come from a drug?

props.label: Who must not get folate alone?

scenes.title: Two ways to make a big cell
scenes.altText: Two cards. Split card: macrocytosis in adults = MCV above 100 fL; megaloblastic causes = deficiency or impaired use of vitamin B12 or folate; nonmegaloblastic causes = myelodysplastic syndrome, liver disease, alcohol, hypothyroidism, certain drugs. Pathway card: B12 is the coenzyme for methionine synthase (homocysteine to methionine), which also regenerates active folate, so B12 lack leaves active folate short and impairs DNA synthesis; B12 is also the coenzyme for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so B12 lack raises methylmalonic acid (MMA).

cues.text: Macrocytosis in adults means an MCV above one hundred femtoliters. The classic split is megaloblastic versus nonmegaloblastic.
Megaloblastic anemia comes from a lack, or impaired use, of vitamin B12 or folate. Nonmegaloblastic causes include myelodysplasia, liver disease, alcohol, hypothyroidism and certain drugs.
Why do both vitamins hit DNA? B12 is the coenzyme that turns homocysteine into methionine, and that same step regenerates active folate. Without B12, active folate runs short too.
B12 has a second job that folate does not share: it is the coenzyme for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Without B12, methylmalonic acid builds up.

scenes.title: B12 is the nerve vitamin
scenes.altText: Two cards. Nerve card: B12 deficiency can cause dysesthesia and, when severe, subacute combined degeneration (ataxia, loss of proprioception and vibration sense); neurologic symptoms are not generally seen in folate deficiency; neurologic or psychiatric disease can occur with no anemia or macrocytosis (40 such patients in the Lindenbaum series), and fewer than 20% of people with low serum B12 have macrocytic anemia. Folate card: folate therapy may mask the anemia, and not treating with cobalamin may accelerate neurologic damage; a high folate status has been shown to worsen the metabolic and clinical consequences of B12 deficiency; some neurologic damage is permanent. Token: check B12 before folate.

cues.text: B12 deficiency can damage nerves: numbness and tingling, and in severe cases subacute combined degeneration, with ataxia and loss of position and vibration sense. Folate deficiency does not generally do this.

The nerves can go first. One series described forty patients with B12-related neurologic or psychiatric disease and no anemia or macrocytosis, and fewer than one in five people with a low B12 have a macrocytic anemia.
Now the trap. Folate can correct the anemia of B12 deficiency and hide it, while the untreated cobalamin lack keeps damaging nerves, and a high folate status can make B12 deficiency worse.
Some of that nerve damage is permanent. So check B12 before treating a megaloblastic anemia with folate alone.

scenes.title: Reading B12, MMA and the drug list
scenes.altText: Four elements. Cutoff card (Nagao 2017): serum B12 below 200 pg/mL = deficiency very likely; above 300 pg/mL = unlikely; 200-300 pg/mL = borderline, use metabolite testing; WHO adult cutoffs below 148 pmol/L deficient, 148-221 pmol/L low. Metabolite card: MMA and homocysteine both rise in B12 deficiency, only homocysteine in folate deficiency; renal insufficiency also raises MMA; normal or falsely high B12 results occur in pernicious anemia with current immunoassays. Hydroxyurea card: inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, impairing DNA synthesis; raises MCV (90-110 fL usually reflects optimized therapy in sickle cell anemia, and MCV trends help track adherence); MCV above 130 fL narrows causes to hydroxyurea, HIV antiretroviral therapy, or B12/folate deficiency; megaloblastic smear features can also appear with drug-induced DNA-synthesis disorders. Hook answers: (1) stop relying on folate alone, measure MMA and treat B12; (2) drug effect, vitamins normal; (3) B12 deficiency without anemia.

cues.text: Reading the B12 level: below two hundred picograms per milliliter, deficiency is very likely; above three hundred, unlikely. Between two and three hundred is borderline.

For borderline values, use the metabolites. Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine both rise in B12 deficiency; only homocysteine rises in folate deficiency. Kidney failure also raises methylmalonic acid.

Drugs cause big cells too. Hydroxyurea blocks ribonucleotide reductase and slows DNA synthesis, so the MCV rises, and an MCV above one hundred thirty points to hydroxyurea, HIV drugs, or vitamin deficiency.
Back to the hook: the first patient needs methylmalonic acid and B12, not folate alone. The second shows a drug effect with normal vitamins. The third has B12 deficiency without anemia.

props.label: Hydroxyurea: blocks DNA synthesis → MCV ↑ (> 130 fL possible)

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Megaloblastic smear, so start folate” (✓ check B12 first; folate can mask the anemia while nerve damage progresses); “A B12 in the reference range rules out deficiency” (✓ 200-300 pg/mL is borderline, use MMA; immunoassays can read normal in pernicious anemia); “Hydroxyurea macrocytosis never looks megaloblastic” (✓ drug-induced DNA-synthesis disorders can show megaloblastic features; rely on normal B12/folate and the drug history).

cues.text: Trap one: the smear looks megaloblastic, so start folate. No: check B12 first, because folate can hide the anemia while nerve damage goes on.
Trap two: a B12 inside the reference range rules out deficiency. No: borderline values need methylmalonic acid, and assays can read normal in pernicious anemia.
Trap three: hydroxyurea macrocytosis never looks megaloblastic. No: drugs that block DNA synthesis can mimic it, so use the vitamin levels and the drug history.

scenes.title: Folate fixes the factory, not the wiring
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Folate fixes the factory, not the wiring.” The marrow factory (DNA synthesis, red cell output) can be patched by folate; the nerve wiring damaged by B12 deficiency is not repaired by folate. Tokens: Factory = DNA, Wiring = nerves, Only B12 fixes both. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: folate fixes the factory, not the wiring. Folate can patch the marrow factory that makes red cells, but only B12 protects the nerve wiring.

Where it breaks: why some people with B12 deficiency get nerve damage and others get anemia is not known, folate deficiency can rarely affect nerves, and drugs such as hydroxyurea also slow the factory.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Check B12 (and MMA if borderline) before folate”, “Hydroxyurea raises the MCV · normal vitamins + drug history”.

cues.text: Before giving folate for a macrocytic anemia, measure vitamin B12 and confirm a borderline level with methylmalonic acid, because folate can hide the anemia while nerve damage progresses, and remember that hydroxyurea can raise the MCV with normal vitamin levels.

props.label: Check B12 (MMA if borderline) before folate
Hydroxyurea raises the MCV · vitamins + drug history

explanation.what: Plain language: big red cells can come from a lack of vitamin B12 or folate, or from other causes such as drugs, alcohol, liver or thyroid disease, or a marrow disorder. B12 deficiency can also harm nerves, and folate given alone can hide the blood clue while the nerve damage continues. Scientific terms: macrocytosis (MCV > 100 fL), megaloblastic anemia, subacute combined degeneration, methionine synthase, methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, methylmalonic acid (MMA), total homocysteine (Hcy), pernicious anemia, ribonucleotide reductase, hydroxyurea.
explanation.why: B12 is the coenzyme for methionine synthase, which converts homocysteine to methionine and regenerates active folate; B12 lack therefore also starves DNA synthesis of active folate. B12 is also the coenzyme for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so MMA rises only in B12 lack. Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, impairing DNA synthesis and raising the MCV.
explanation.measure: Serum B12 < 200 pg/mL: deficiency very likely; > 300 pg/mL: unlikely; 200–300 pg/mL: borderline, use metabolites (Nagao 2017). WHO adult cutoffs: < 148 pmol/L deficient, 148–221 pmol/L low. MMA and Hcy both rise in B12 deficiency, only Hcy in folate deficiency; renal insufficiency raises MMA; Hcy also rises with B6 deficiency, renal impairment and hypothyroidism. Serum B12 can read normal or falsely high in pernicious anemia with current immunoassays. On hydroxyurea for sickle cell anemia, an MCV of 90–110 fL usually reflects optimized therapy; MCV above 130 fL narrows causes to hydroxyurea, HIV antiretroviral therapy, or B12/folate deficiency.
explanation.differs: B12 deficiency (MMA and Hcy up, nerve damage possible even without anemia) vs folate deficiency (Hcy up, MMA normal, nerve damage not generally seen) vs drug-induced macrocytosis (normal B12 and folate, drug history; smear features can overlap with megaloblastic anemia).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: choose MMA for a borderline B12, refuse folate monotherapy in a megaloblastic anemia with neurologic signs, pick the analyte that separates B12 from folate deficiency, or attribute macrocytosis to hydroxyurea when vitamins are normal.

mnemonic.text: Folate fixes the factory, not the wiring: folate can patch the marrow factory that makes red cells, but only B12 protects the nerve wiring.
mnemonic.explanation: Reminds you that correcting the anemia with folate does not treat the neurologic risk of B12 deficiency.
mnemonic.limitation: Why some B12-deficient patients develop nerve damage and others anemia is unknown; neurologic symptoms are “not generally” (not never) seen in folate deficiency; drugs such as hydroxyurea also slow the factory without any vitamin lack.

analogyLimitations: The factory and wiring picture simplifies a metabolic mechanism that is not fully understood.
takeaway: Before giving folate for a macrocytic anemia, measure vitamin B12 and confirm a borderline level with methylmalonic acid, because folate can hide the anemia while nerve damage progresses, and remember that hydroxyurea can raise the MCV with normal vitamin levels.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has MCV 112 fL, macro-ovalocytes, numb feet and an unsteady gait. Serum B12 is 240 pg/mL and serum folate is low-normal. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Measure methylmalonic acid and do not treat with folate alone
options.rationale: Correct. 200–300 pg/mL is borderline; MMA rises in B12 deficiency, and folate alone can mask the anemia while nerve damage progresses.

options.text: Start folic acid alone and recheck the blood count in a month
options.rationale: Incorrect. Folate can correct the anemia of B12 deficiency and hide it while untreated cobalamin lack keeps damaging nerves.

options.text: Conclude B12 deficiency is excluded because the result is above 200 pg/mL
options.rationale: Incorrect. Values of 200–300 pg/mL are borderline, and serum B12 can read normal in pernicious anemia.

options.text: Measure homocysteine alone to decide between B12 and folate deficiency
options.rationale: Incorrect. Homocysteine rises in both B12 and folate deficiency, so it cannot separate them; MMA rises only in B12 deficiency.

questions.stem: A man taking hydroxyurea for essential thrombocythemia has MCV 118 fL. Serum B12 and folate are normal. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, impairing DNA synthesis, and commonly raises the MCV
options.rationale: Correct. Hydroxyurea is a ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor and is a recognized cause of drug-induced macrocytosis.

options.text: Finding hypersegmented neutrophils would exclude a drug cause
options.rationale: Incorrect. Megaloblastic smear features can also be seen in drug-induced disorders of DNA synthesis.

options.text: He has occult folate deficiency and should start folic acid
options.rationale: Incorrect. Folate is normal and there is a clear drug explanation; folate given without excluding B12 deficiency is also hazardous.

options.text: An MCV above 130 fL would rule out hydroxyurea as the cause
options.rationale: Incorrect. Hydroxyurea is one of the few causes of an MCV above 130 fL, with HIV antiretroviral therapy and B12 or folate deficiency.

questions.stem: Which result is raised in vitamin B12 deficiency but NOT in folate deficiency (assuming normal renal function)?

options.rationale: Correct. MMA accumulates when B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase fails; renal insufficiency can also raise it.
Incorrect. Homocysteine rises in both B12 and folate deficiency.
Incorrect. Both deficiencies cause megaloblastic, macrocytic anemia, and B12 deficiency does not always raise the MCV.
Incorrect. RBC folate reflects tissue folate stores; it is a folate measure, not a marker raised by B12 deficiency.

claims.text: Macrocytosis = MCV > 100 fL; megaloblastic (B12/folate) vs nonmegaloblastic causes.
B12 coenzyme for methionine synthase (regenerating active folate) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMA).

B12 deficiency causes neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration, not generally seen in folate deficiency; can occur without anemia or macrocytosis; fewer than 20% with low B12 have macrocytic anemia; damage can be permanent.
Folate therapy may mask the anemia while untreated B12 deficiency accelerates neurologic damage; high folate status worsens B12 deficiency.
Serum B12 cutoffs (< 200, 200–300, > 300 pg/mL; WHO < 148 and 148–221 pmol/L); assay failures in pernicious anemia.
MMA and Hcy both up in B12 deficiency, only Hcy in folate deficiency; renal insufficiency raises MMA; RBC folate reflects tissue stores.

Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and raises MCV (90–110 fL usually optimized in sickle cell anemia; MCV tracks adherence); MCV > 130 fL causes; megaloblastic features can occur in drug-induced DNA-synthesis disorders.
Folate cannot rescue the methionine/SAM pathway needed for myelin; hydroxyurea macrocytosis lacks hypersegmented neutrophils; review TSH before chasing B12.
claims.note: Not supported by the sources read and not taught. Wolffenbuttel 2019 states the reason some patients present with nerve damage and others with anemia is unknown; Nagao 2017 says megaloblastic morphology can also be seen in drug-induced DNA-synthesis disorders and begins the workup with B12, folate and the smear.

claims.text: Scenario invented; cards and pathways schematic.
“Folate fixes the factory, not the wiring.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 33 Hit 3 (and the Number Vault) gives deficiency as usually < 100 ng/L and borderline B12 as 100–200 ng/L. Nagao 2017 states deficiency is very likely below 200 pg/mL (= ng/L) and puts the borderline zone at 200–300 pg/mL; Wolffenbuttel 2019 uses 140–300 pmol/L; WHO cutoffs are < 148 pmol/L deficient and 148–221 pmol/L low (Hannibal 2016). Serum B12 can also read normal in pernicious anemia (register flag rv-ch33-b12-borderline-range).

Ch. 33 Hit 16 calls hydroxyurea macrocytosis nonmegaloblastic with no hypersegmented neutrophils. Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and impairs DNA synthesis (Green 2014), and Nagao 2017 states macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils may also be seen in drug-induced disorders of DNA synthesis, so the smear does not reliably exclude a drug cause (register flag rv-ch33-hydroxyurea-not-reliably-nonmegaloblastic).

Ch. 33 Hit 16 advises reviewing medications and TSH before chasing B12. Nagao 2017 begins the macrocytosis workup with serum B12, folate and the smear, and considers hypothyroidism among nonmegaloblastic causes once vitamin deficiency is excluded and reticulocytes are not raised (register flag rv-ch33-macrocytosis-first-tests).
